# Memory in mechanisms {#sec-memory}

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" icon="false"}
**Status:** draft · **Updated:** 2026-11-25 · **Checked by:** `tests/test_bistable.py`, `tests/test_bitbody.py`, `tests/test_erasure.py`
:::

Everything before this chapter is linear. A linear body forgets: whatever the environment
does to it fades on the body's own relaxation time. Computation needs memory, a record that
outlasts the event, and that needs a nonlinear body. This chapter takes the simplest one, an
element with two stable shapes, and follows a single bit through its life.

The answers, in plain terms:

- *A barrier keeps a record exponentially longer.* An element with two wells keeps which
    well it is in until thermal noise carries it over the barrier, a time that grows like
    $e^{\Delta E/\sigma_T^2}$. A linear element forgets the same push in a few relaxation
    times. For a body whose future depends only on its present state, a window of its
    history holds exactly what its state at the start of the window holds about the past,
    so memory is the state carrying the past forward (@sec-bit).
- *Writing takes a sustained push.* A sharp kick that crosses the barrier usually bounces
    back. A steady push beyond a critical force removes the starting well and writes the bit
    reliably, for a few barriers of work (@sec-write).
- *Other parts read the bit through a load path.* The stored bit shifts the body's static
    shape. A part reads it only if pushing on that part would load the element, and the
    body's push-back that makes the bit readable also lowers its barrier (@sec-bit-body).
- *Erasing has a floor.* Resetting a bit of unknown value costs at least $\sigma_T^2\ln2$
    (Landauer). A slow erasure reaches it, but leaves more errors; in a full cycle, the
    environment's push dominates the cost (@sec-erase).

The results were first recorded as dated research notes, which the research log keeps.

## A mechanical bit {#sec-bit}

### The element

One coordinate $x$ of mass $m$ in the double well
$$
V(x)=\Delta E\big((x/a)^2-1\big)^2 ,
$$
with wells at $x=\pm a$ and a barrier $\Delta E$ at $x=0$, damping rate $\gamma=b/m$, and the
Langevin body's thermal force, so that the Gibbs law is $\propto\exp\!\big(-(V+\tfrac12m\dot x^2)/\sigma_T^2\big)$
(@sec-langevin). Lengths are in $a$, energies in $\sigma_T^2$ and times in
$\sqrt{ma^2/\sigma_T^2}$; the barrier is $\beta=\Delta E/\sigma_T^2$ and $\gamma=2$. Near a
well the energy metric is the local quadratic one, with stiffness $V''(\pm a)=8\Delta E/a^2$.

**What the wells are.** The double well is the simplest form of any snap-through element
near the point where it becomes bistable. A thin strip squeezed from its ends bows up or
down; $x$ is the midpoint deflection, the wells are the two bowed shapes, and the barrier
is the extra strain energy of the straight, compressed shape the strip must pass through,
set by how hard the ends are squeezed. Shallow domes (a jumping-popper toy, a vacuum lid),
two-bar snap-through linkages, latches and detents, snap-through grippers and the bistable
cells of mechanical metamaterials behave the same way. The book's $\sigma_T^2=10^{-4}$ J is
an effective temperature standing for mechanical disturbances such as vibration and
impacts, not molecular motion, which carries about $4\times10^{-21}$ J; against that, a
macroscopic strip would keep its bit indefinitely. On the book's scale a barrier of
$10\,\sigma_T^2$ is 1 mJ, about the snap-through energy of a small buckled steel strip. The
question here is therefore how long such an element keeps a record against a given level
of disturbance.

The environment writes one bit $E$: at $t=0$ it either pushed the element into the right
well or did not, with equal odds. The write is taken to be perfect. The comparison is a
harmonic element with the stiffness of one well, $k=8\Delta E/a^2$, and the same damping,
pushed by the same displacement $2a$.

::: {#prp-bit-decay name="How a bit in a well decays"}
Treat the well, left or right, as a two-state record that flips at rate $r$ in each
direction. After a time $t$ it holds
$$
I(t)=1-h\Big(\tfrac12\big(1-e^{-2rt}\big)\Big)\ \text{bits}
$$
about the written bit, where $h$ is the binary entropy. It falls to half a bit at
$t_{1/2}=0.124/r$.
:::

::: {.proof}
For a two-state chain that flips at rate $r$ each way, the probability of being in the
other state after time $t$ is $p(t)=\frac12(1-e^{-2rt})$: the difference of the two
occupation probabilities decays at rate $2r$. The record is the written bit passed through
a binary symmetric channel with crossover $p(t)$, which carries $1-h(p)$ bits. Half a bit
is reached at $h(p)=\frac12$, so $p=0.110$ and $t_{1/2}=-\log(1-2p)/(2r)=0.124/r$.
:::

The two-state picture holds when flips are rare compared with the motion inside a well,
which is true for barriers of a few $\sigma_T^2$ and more. The well is a coarse record:
the full state $(x,\dot x)$ can hold slightly more, mainly during a crossing, so $I(t)$ is a
lower bound on what the state holds.

For the flip rate, Kramers' formula for moderate to strong damping
[@kramers1940brownian; @hanggi1990reaction] gives
$$
r=\frac{\omega_0}{2\pi\omega_b}\Big(\sqrt{\gamma^2/4+\omega_b^2}-\gamma/2\Big)e^{-\Delta E/\sigma_T^2},
\qquad\omega_0^2=\frac{8\Delta E}{ma^2},\ \ \omega_b^2=\frac{4\Delta E}{ma^2}.
$$
It is an approximation that becomes exact as the barrier grows. Simulations of 4,000
elements, started in the right well and integrated with a standard Langevin scheme
(BAOAB), give rates 7% to 15% below the formula for barriers of 3 to 8 $\sigma_T^2$
(@tbl-kramers).

::: {#prp-linear-forgets name="A linear element forgets on its relaxation time"}
For the harmonic element, the push is recorded by the shift $\mu(t)$ of the state's mean,
measured against the Gibbs covariance as the separation $d(t)$. The record holds
$$
I(t)=1-\E\big[\log_2(1+e^{-L})\big],\qquad L\sim\mathcal N\big(d^2/2,\;d^2\big),
$$
bits, which depends only on $d(t)$. The separation decays with the element's relaxation,
so the time to fall to half a bit grows only like the logarithm of the initial separation.
:::

::: {.proof name="Proof sketch"}
With and without the push, the state at time $t$ is Gaussian with the same covariance (the
Gibbs law) and means that differ by $\mu(t)=e^{At}(2a,0)^\top$. For two equally likely
Gaussians with a common covariance, the log-likelihood ratio $L$ is Gaussian with mean
$d^2/2$ and variance $d^2$ under the hypothesis that holds, with $d^2=\mu^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mu$, and
the information is $1-\E[\log_2(1+e^{-L})]$. The mean decays with envelope $e^{-\gamma t/2}$,
so $d(t)\approx d(0)e^{-\gamma t/2}$, and $d$ reaches the value that gives half a bit after a
time $\frac2\gamma\log\big(d(0)/d_{1/2}\big)$. Here $d(0)=\sqrt{32\beta}$ grows only like
$\sqrt\beta$. The element oscillates, so $I(t)$ wiggles as it falls; the half-life is taken
at the first time it reaches half a bit.
:::

::: {#prp-markov-window name="A window of history holds what its first state holds"}
Let the body's state $X_t$ (positions and velocities) be a Markov process, and let an event
$E$ happen at time 0. For any $0<s<t$, the history on $[s,t]$ holds
$$
I\big(E;\,X_{[s,t]}\big)=I(E;\,X_s),
$$
and $I(E;X_s)$ cannot increase with $s$.
:::

::: {.proof}
The window contains $X_s$, so by the chain rule
$I(E;X_{[s,t]})=I(E;X_s)+I(E;X_{(s,t]}\mid X_s)$. Given $X_s$, the later states do not
depend on anything before $s$, the event included (Markov property), so the second term is
zero. For $s<s'$ the chain $E\to X_s\to X_{s'}$ and data processing give
$I(E;X_{s'})\le I(E;X_s)$.
:::

On the rigid leg, with a force impulse of Gaussian amplitude at $t=0$, a 20 ms window of
the whole state holds 0.5146, 0.2368 and 0.0148 bits when it starts 2, 10 and 30 ms after
the impulse. The state at the start of each window holds the same, to $10^{-9}$
(`check_window`). The proposition needs the whole state. If only some coordinates are
observed, or the thermal bath has its own hidden state, as in the bath with memory of the
[research note on payload mass](../notes/2026-11-22-mass-and-resolution.qmd), a window can hold more than the observed coordinates at its start.

## Writing the bit {#sec-write}

The element is that of @sec-bit: one coordinate in the double well $V(x)=\Delta E((x/a)^2-1)^2$,
damping rate $\gamma=2$, the Langevin body's thermal noise, units of $a$, $\sigma_T^2$ and
$\sqrt{ma^2/\sigma_T^2}$. Elements start in the left well, drawn from the Gibbs law. The
environment either does nothing or pushes toward the right well, with equal odds. Two kinds
of push:

- a *sharp kick*, an impulse $J$ that adds $J/m$ to the velocity, given in units of
    $\sqrt{2m\Delta E}$, the impulse whose kinetic energy equals the barrier;
- a *steady push*, a constant force $F$ held for 3 time units and then released, given in
    units of $F_c$.

The element is read 8 time units after the push ends, long compared with the motion inside
a well and short compared with spontaneous flips at high barriers. The result is the chance
$q_1$ of finding it in the right well after a push, and $q_0$ without one. The bits the well
records about the push are
$$
I=h\big(\tfrac12(q_0+q_1)\big)-\tfrac12\big(h(q_0)+h(q_1)\big),
$$
the information through a binary channel with equal priors, where $h$ is the binary
entropy.

::: {#prp-kick-threshold name="A kick needs the barrier's energy"}
Without thermal noise, a kick of impulse $J$ on an element resting at the bottom of a well
can carry it into the other well only if $J^2/(2m)\ge\Delta E$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Right after the kick the element's energy is $J^2/(2m)$, since the bottom of the well has
$V=0$. Without noise, damping can only remove energy. Reaching the top of the barrier at
$x=0$ needs energy at least $V(0)=\Delta E$.
:::

Noise blurs this threshold: at 8 thermal energies a kick with exactly the barrier's energy
succeeds 21% of the time. Damping makes it worse than the bound suggests, because energy is
lost on the way up, and a stronger kick overshoots: the element crosses with energy to spare,
reaches the far wall of the right well and comes back. The chance of success peaks near 89%
for a kick carrying 4 barriers of energy and falls to 31% at 9.

::: {#prp-critical-force name="Above a critical force the starting well disappears"}
Under a steady force $F>0$ toward the right well, the left well survives only while
$$
F<F_c=\frac{8\,\Delta E}{3\sqrt3\,a}.
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
With the force, the potential is $V(x)-Fx$, and its stationary points solve $V'(x)=F$. On
the left, between the left well's bottom and the barrier, $V'(x)=4\beta x(x^2-1)$ in the
book's units. It is positive there and largest at $x=-1/\sqrt3$, where it equals
$8\beta/(3\sqrt3)$. For $F$ below that value, $V'(x)=F$ has a solution with
$V''>0$ on the left: a well. Above it there is none, and the element slides to the right.
:::

Without noise, a steady push just above $F_c$ held long enough writes the bit every time.
With noise, the chance rises steeply around $F_c$ (@fig-write(b)): at 8 thermal energies it
is 12% at half the critical force, 96% at $F_c$ and 98.5% to 99.4% from 1.1 to 1.6 times
$F_c$. Far above $F_c$ the element is pushed so far that, on release, it falls back with
enough energy to recross sometimes (98% at $2F_c$).

::: {#rem-write-cost name="The cost grows with the log of the lifetime"}
A reliable write takes about $c\,\Delta E$ of work, with $c\approx3.6$ at 98.5% reliability
here, and all of it is dissipated, since the element ends in a well at the same energy as it
started. The bit's lifetime grows like $e^{\Delta E/\sigma_T^2}$ (@prp-bit-decay with
Kramers' rate). So, to keep a bit $e$ times longer, the barrier rises by $\sigma_T^2$ and the
write costs about $3.6\,\sigma_T^2$ more. This is a measured constant, not a bound. Landauer's
bound of $\sigma_T^2\ln2$ [@landauer1961irreversibility] concerns erasing a bit whose value is
unknown, which this element needs before it can record the next event; writing into a known
starting state, as here, is not bounded by it.
:::

## A bit inside a body {#sec-bit-body}

In a robot the element is part of a body. This section asks what the other parts of the
body hold about the bit, and whether being in a body changes the bit itself. The body is the
clamped SEA on the book's ground, in joint coordinates $q=(\theta_j,\theta_m)$, with the
Langevin body's thermal noise at $\sigma_T^2=10^{-4}$ J. A bistable element with energy
$V(z)=\Delta E\big((z/a)^2-1\big)^2$ acts on one coordinate $z=a_e^\top q$, with its own damper
at 10% of critical. Two placements:

- *series*: the element replaces the series spring, $z=\theta_j-\theta_m$, with stiffness
    $k_w=8\Delta E/a^2=10^3$ N m/rad at the bottom of a well, like the book's SEA;
- *latch*: the element holds the rotor against the frame, $z=\theta_m$, alongside a series
    spring of $10^3$ N m/rad, with $k_w=10^4$ N m/rad.

$K_0$ and $D$ are the body's stiffness and damping without the element's spring. In each
placement the element's own barrier is chosen so that element and body together have a
barrier of $8\,\sigma_T^2$.

::: {#prp-bit-shift name="The wells of element and body together"}
Hold the element at $z$. The rest of the body settles at $q=z\,u$, where $u$ minimizes
$u^\top K_0u$ subject to $a_e^\top u=1$, and adds the energy $\frac12k_{\rm eff}z^2$ with
$k_{\rm eff}=u^\top K_0u$. Element and body are bistable exactly when $k_{\rm eff}<k_w/2$. Then,
with $c=2k_{\rm eff}/k_w$, the wells sit at $z_w=\pm a\sqrt{1-c}$, the barrier is
$\Delta E(1-c)^2$, and the stored bit moves the body by $2z_w\,u$.
:::

::: {.proof}
*Step 1: the body follows.* The energy is $U(q)=\frac12q^\top K_0q+V(a_e^\top q)$. At fixed
$z=a_e^\top q$ the second term is fixed, so the body minimizes $\frac12q^\top K_0q$ under the
linear constraint $a_e^\top q=z$. The minimizer scales with $z$: $q=z\,u$. The minimum is
$\frac12k_{\rm eff}z^2$.

*Step 2: the effective double well.* What remains is
$U_{\rm eff}(z)=\frac12k_{\rm eff}z^2+\Delta E\big((z/a)^2-1\big)^2$. Its derivative vanishes at
$z=0$ and where $z^2/a^2=1-k_{\rm eff}a^2/(4\Delta E)=1-c$, using $k_w=8\Delta E/a^2$. These are
wells only when $c<1$.

*Step 3: the barrier.* With $s=1-c$, $U_{\rm eff}(z_w)=\frac12k_{\rm eff}a^2s+\Delta E\,c^2
=\Delta E\,(2cs+c^2)=\Delta E(2c-c^2)$, and $U_{\rm eff}(0)=\Delta E$. The difference is
$\Delta E(1-c)^2$. Because the body was minimized out at each $z$, this is the lowest
barrier between the two wells of the full body.
:::

::: {#cor-load-path name="A part reads the bit only through a load path"}
The bit moves part $p$ by $\Delta_p=2z_w\,u_p$. When $K_0$ is invertible,
$$
u_p=\frac{a_e^\top K_0^{-1}p}{a_e^\top K_0^{-1}a_e},
$$
and $a_e^\top K_0^{-1}p$ is how much the element's coordinate moves when the part is pushed
with the element removed. So a part reads the bit exactly when pushing on it would load the
element. If nothing in the body resists the element ($k_{\rm eff}=0$), the barrier is the
element's own, and every part whose push does not reach the element reads nothing.
:::

::: {.proof}
With $K_0$ invertible, the constrained minimizer of Step 1 is $u=K_0^{-1}a_e/(a_e^\top K_0^{-1}a_e)$
(Lagrange multipliers). Its component along $p$ is the stated ratio, and
$a_e^\top K_0^{-1}p$ is the change in $z$ under the static push $p$, by reciprocity
($K_0^{-1}$ is symmetric). When $K_0$ is singular, as with the SEA's free rotor, the same
minimization is solved directly; a zero-energy motion that changes $z$ gives $k_{\rm eff}=0$.
:::

On the SEA with the series element, the rotor is free, so the body does not resist the
element at all: $k_{\rm eff}=0$, the wells stay at $\pm a$, and $u=(0,-1)$. The rotor moves by
$2a=5.06\times10^{-3}$ rad and the link by exactly zero. Pushing on the link moves the rotor
along with it and never stretches the element. With the latch, the series spring and the
ground resist the rotor with $k_{\rm eff}=909$ N m/rad, the barrier drops by
$(1-c)^2=0.67$, and the bit moves the link by $1.61\times10^{-4}$ rad and the rotor by
$1.77\times10^{-3}$ rad.

::: {#prp-read-rate name="How fast a part reads the bit"}
Linearize about a well, with stiffness $K=K_0+V''(z_w)\,a_ea_e^\top$. The two bits give the
part Gaussian histories with the same covariance and means $\pm\Delta_p/2$. A snapshot
separates them by $d^2=\Delta_p^2/(\sigma_T^2\,p^\top K^{-1}p)$, and over a long window $T$
$$
d^2(T)\approx\frac{\Delta_p^2}{\sigma_T^2\,p^\top x}+T\,\frac{\Delta_p^2}{2\sigma_T^2\,x^\top Dx},
\qquad x=K^{-1}p .
$$
The bits read are those of a binary choice between two Gaussians at separation $d$.
:::

::: {.proof name="Proof sketch"}
*The snapshot.* By the Gibbs law the part's position has variance $\sigma_T^2p^\top K^{-1}p$
in either well, and the means differ by $\Delta_p$.

*The window.* A constant difference $\Delta_p$ seen through stationary Gaussian noise with
zero-frequency spectral density $S(0)$ gives $d^2\approx T\Delta_p^2/S(0)$ for a long window.
By fluctuation-dissipation the part's spectrum is $2\sigma_T^2\,p^\top YDY^*p$, and at zero
frequency $Y=K^{-1}$, so $S(0)=2\sigma_T^2\,x^\top Dx$.

*What is not proved here.* The cross-over between the two regimes; the exact finite-window
values are computed directly below.
:::

$x^\top Dx$ is the sum of every damper's coefficient times its stretch squared under a static
push at the part. This is the push-on-the-part rule of @sec-inside again, now at zero
frequency and with the stored bit as the source: dampers that a push at the part stretches
add noise to its reading.

## Erasing the bit, and the cost of a cycle {#sec-erase}

A body that records events over and over must clear each record before it can take the
next one. The element is that of @sec-bit, in the book's units (lengths $a$, energies $\sigma_T^2$, times
$\sqrt{ma^2/\sigma_T^2}$), damping rate $\gamma=2$, written as
$$
U(x,t)=\beta x^4-a_2(t)\,x^2-f(t)\,x ,
$$
which is the double well $\beta\big((x^2-1)^2-1\big)$ with barrier $\beta=8$ when
$a_2=2\beta$ and $f=0$. The bit starts in a random well, each with probability one half, at
equilibrium inside its well. The erasure resets it to the left well in four stages of equal
length $\tau$ [@berut2012experimental]:

1. lower the barrier, $a_2$ from $2\beta$ to 0;
2. tilt to the left, $f$ from 0 to $-5$, so that the right side ends 10 thermal energies
    higher;
3. raise the barrier, $a_2$ from 0 back to $2\beta$;
4. remove the tilt, $f$ from $-5$ to 0.

The work is the energy put in by changing the potential, summed along each trajectory as
$U(x,t+dt)-U(x,t)$ at the current position. Each value of $\tau$ uses 2,000 elements.

::: {#prp-landauer name="Landauer's bound, with errors"}
Reset an element whose well is equally likely to be left or right, so that afterwards it is
in the right well with probability $p\le\frac12$, and both wells have the same shape at the
start and the end. The mean work satisfies
$$
\langle W\rangle\ \ge\ \sigma_T^2\big(\ln2-H(p)\big),\qquad H(p)=-p\ln p-(1-p)\ln(1-p),
$$
which is $\sigma_T^2\ln2$ for a perfect reset.
:::

::: {.proof name="Proof sketch"}
*Step 1: the second law far from equilibrium.* For the Langevin body with a potential
changed in time, the mean work exceeds the change in nonequilibrium free energy,
$\langle W\rangle\ge\Delta\mathcal F$, where $\mathcal F=\langle U\rangle-\sigma_T^2S$ and $S$ is
the entropy of the distribution of the state [@esposito2011second]. The difference is
$\sigma_T^2$ times the entropy produced, which is never negative.

*Step 2: the start and the end.* The potential is the same at both ends. Inside each well
the element is at local equilibrium, and the two wells are mirror images, so the mean
energy is the same before and after. Only the occupation of the wells changes: from
$(\frac12,\frac12)$, with entropy $\ln2$, to $(1-p,p)$, with entropy $H(p)$. So
$\Delta\mathcal F=\sigma_T^2(\ln2-H(p))$.

*What is not proved here.* Step 1 is quoted; the end state is taken to be at local
equilibrium inside each well, which holds when the barrier is high.
:::

The bound counts the work against the information the body loses about where the element
could be. Writing into a known starting state, as in @sec-write, loses no such
information, and Landauer's bound does not apply to it. Reading the bit by another part of
the body, as in @sec-bit-body, needs no work at all: the part simply moves with the
body. That is the classical position of Bennett [@bennett1982thermodynamics]: measuring can be
free, and the cost appears when a record is erased.

## What this chapter shows {#sec-memory-summary}

A two-well element gives a body what no linear body has: a record that lasts. The record
survives for a time exponential in the barrier over the thermal energy, it is written by a
push that lasts long enough to remove the starting well, it is read by any part whose load
path runs through the element, and it is cleared at a cost of at least $\sigma_T^2\ln2$.
Each step has a price in energy or in stability. Being readable lowers the barrier, a
reliable write costs a few barriers, a slow erasure leaks. These are the first pieces of
mechanical computation in the book, and they connect mechanical intelligence to the
thermodynamics of computation.

**What wells are, physically.** Snap-through elements: strips squeezed into a bow, shallow
domes, two-bar linkages, latches and the bistable cells of mechanical metamaterials
(@sec-bit). The book's $\sigma_T^2$ is an effective temperature standing for mechanical
disturbances such as vibration and impacts.

**Limits.**

- One coordinate for the element, symmetric wells, and the book's SEA as the body.
- Kramers' rate is an approximation; the simulations are the reference.
- The well is used as the record, a lower bound on what the full state holds.
- One write protocol and one erasure protocol; optimal protocols are not explored.

**Open.** A part watching while the bit is written; erasing a bit inside a body; stiffening
and other nonlinear springs; several bits, and simple logic between them.
